m1-internet-vs-www: People often mix up the Internet and the World Wide Web, but they are actually two separate layers. Think of the Internet as a global highway system made of fiber cables, towers, and routers moving data around. The World Wide Web is simply one bus line riding on those highways, carrying linked pages to your browser. Apps like WhatsApp and email travel on the Internet directly without using the Web at all. So remember: without the Internet, nothing connects, while without the Web, messaging and email still work just fine.
m1-url-dns-ip: Computers don't look up websites by name. Instead, they find servers using numeric I P addresses, much like a street number. Since memorizing strings of numbers is tough for humans, the web relies on D N S, the Domain Name System, which works like the Internet's phone book. When you enter an address like druba dot in, your browser reads the protocol, domain, and path, then asks D N S for the matching I P address. Once D N S replies, your browser connects straight to the server and loads the page.
m1-how-web-works: Every time you visit a webpage, your browser and a web server have a quick back-and-forth chat over H T T P. Your browser sends a request, usually a GET request to fetch a page or a POST request to submit form data. The server replies with a status code like 200 when everything succeeds, or 404 when a page is missing. Think of plain H T T P like a postcard anyone can read, whereas H T T P S seals your data inside an encrypted envelope. Always look for H T T P S before entering a password.
m1-architecture: A modern website works a lot like a restaurant. The Front End is the dining hall you see and interact with inside your browser. H T M L builds the structure, C S S styles the layout and colors, and JavaScript adds interactivity. The Back End is the kitchen behind the scenes, running on a server to handle logins and database queries. Responsive design lets that same dining hall adapt smoothly, so your site feels comfortable on both a small phone and a wide desktop screen.
m1-first-page: You don't need any special software to create your first webpage. Every webpage is simply a plain text file saved with a dot H T M L extension. Name your main home page index dot H T M L, since web servers look for that filename automatically, and keep other pages lowercase with hyphens instead of spaces. Behind-the-scenes details like the title belong in the head section, while everything visitors see goes inside the body. Always save your file before refreshing the browser so your latest edits appear.
m2-text-headings: H T M L gives your text clear meaning rather than just changing its font size. Think of your page like a newspaper outline: use one h-1 tag for the main headline, then step down through h-2 to h-6 for sub-sections. Always nest tags properly by closing the innermost tag before the outer one. When you need extra emphasis, H T M L 5 offers helpful formatting tags like strong for importance, mark for highlighting, and sub or sup for formulas. Choose tags for document structure first, and leave visual styling to C S S.
m2-links-images: Hyperlinks and images bring a webpage to life. Anchor tags connect pages together using the h-ref attribute, and adding target equals underscore blank opens external sites neatly in a new tab. Images use the self-closing image tag with a source path, and they should always include a descriptive alt attribute. Think of alt text as a spoken caption: it helps screen readers describe the visual and acts as a fallback if the image ever fails to load. Make adding alt text an automatic habit.
m2-lists: Whenever you want to group related items, H T M L gives you unordered lists for bullets and ordered lists for numbered or lettered steps. You can even customize ordered lists with type and start attributes to begin counting from any letter or number. The one rule beginners trip over is nesting sub-lists. Think of lists like computer folders: a sub-folder belongs inside a main folder, never floating between two items. So always place a nested list inside its parent list item tag before closing it.
m2-tables: H T M L tables organize structured data into rows and columns using table, row, header, and data cell tags. To build clean layouts like schedules or report cards, you will often merge cells just like in a spreadsheet. Use colspan to stretch a cell horizontally across several columns, such as a banner title at the top. Use rowspan to stretch a cell vertically down multiple rows. Just remember one key detail: whenever a cell spans downward with rowspan, the rows underneath need one fewer cell to stay aligned.
m2-forms: Forms are how websites collect information from visitors, from search bars to sign-up pages. Pair every input with a matching label so users and screen readers know exactly what to type, and give radio buttons the same name attribute so only one choice can be picked at a time. Use the GET method for simple searches, and POST for logins or private details. H T M L 5 also gives you free built-in validation using input types like email along with the required attribute to catch mistakes right away.
m2-semantics-iframes: You could build an entire page out of generic div tags, but that is like stacking unlabeled moving boxes. Semantic H T M L 5 tags such as header, nav, main, article, and footer label every region clearly. That makes your page far easier for both search engines and screen readers to navigate. For media and external embeds, use native audio and video tags with the controls attribute, and use an iframe when embedding another page. Keeping your structure semantic makes your code cleaner and much more accessible.
m3-vars-operators: In modern JavaScript, store values with const by default, and switch to let only when a value needs to change later. Avoid the older var keyword, and use typeof whenever you want to inspect a value's data type. Watch out for two classic beginner traps: adding a string and a number joins them as text instead of doing math, and loose double-equals ignores data types. Make it a habit to convert text inputs with Number first, and always compare values using strict triple-equals so your logic stays predictable.
m3-popup-boxes: JavaScript includes three built-in dialog boxes for quick user interaction, much like a front reception desk. Alert simply displays a short announcement with an O K button. Confirm asks a yes-or-no question and returns true for O K or false for Cancel. Prompt asks the user to type a short answer and returns their text, or null if they cancel. One quick reminder: prompt always returns a string, even if the user types digits, so wrap numeric replies in Number before doing any math with them.
m3-control-flow: Control flow lets your code make decisions and repeat work automatically. Think of if-else and switch statements like railway switches that send execution down one track based on a condition. When using switch, always include a break at the end of each case so execution doesn't accidentally fall into the next one. For repeating tasks, use a for loop when you know the exact count, a while loop to check before running, and a do-while loop when the code must run at least once before checking.
m3-try-catch: Even well-written code can run into surprises like bad user input or missing data. Wrapping risky operations in a try-catch block acts like a safety net during a stunt: your code runs inside try, and if anything goes wrong, execution jumps safely into catch instead of crashing the whole script. You can also use throw with a new Error to enforce your own custom rules, and add a finally block for cleanup steps that must run every time. Always show helpful error messages instead of failing silently.
m3-builtin-es6: You rarely need to build everyday utilities from scratch in JavaScript because handy built-in objects are already ready to use. Arrays store ordered lists starting at index zero, with powerful helpers like push, map, and filter. The Date object reads the live clock and calendar, though remember that months are zero-based, so January is zero. The Math object handles rounding, maximums, and random numbers like rolling a die. Combine these with modern template literals and arrow functions to keep your code clean and readable.
m4-css-types-selectors: You can add C S S to a webpage in three ways: inline on a single tag, internally inside a style block, or externally in a shared stylesheet. External stylesheets are best because one file keeps your entire site consistent. When two C S S rules target the same element, specificity decides the winner. Think of it like clothing: a tag selector is a basic uniform, a class is a team jersey, an I D is a unique badge, and an inline style overrides them all. Stick mostly to reusable classes so your styles stay easy to manage.
m4-box-model-div-span: In C S S, every single element on the page is treated like a rectangular box made of four layers. Picture a framed photo hanging on a wall: your text or image is the content, padding is the inner mat around it, border is the picture frame, and margin is the empty wall space separating it from other frames. Div elements stack as full-width blocks while spans flow inline within text. Using box-sizing set to border-box is a great habit because it keeps padding and borders neatly inside your chosen width.
m4-layout-effects: Flexbox makes aligning elements in rows or columns remarkably simple once you remember one golden rule: apply display flex to the parent container, not the child items inside it. Picture organizing books on a shelf: justify-content controls how items space out along the main direction, while align-items lines up their height across the shelf. Pair Flexbox with sticky positioning for headers that stay visible while scrolling, and use media queries to adjust your layout cleanly as screen sizes grow from phones to desktops.
m4-dom-dhtml: Once a browser loads your H T M L, it builds a live tree of elements in memory called the DOM, or Document Object Model. Think of H T M L as building the stage once, while the DOM lets JavaScript change text, swap styles, and react to clicks while the show is live. Use addEventListener to listen for user actions cleanly. And when updating text on screen, remember the difference between inner H T M L and textContent: inner H T M L renders tags, while textContent safely displays plain text and protects against script injection.
m5-security-overview: Good web security rests on three core pillars called the C I A Triad. Picture an armored bank vault: Confidentiality locks data away from eavesdroppers using H T T P S encryption, Integrity seals records so nobody can tamper with them in transit, and Availability keeps the vault doors open for real users. Two common attacks to guard against are cross-site scripting, where attackers sneak scripts into unsafe inner H T M L, and S Q L injection against databases. Sanitizing input, preferring textContent, and enforcing H T T P S cover the essentials.
m5-firewalls: A firewall acts as a protective checkpoint controlling traffic between your server and the public Internet. Think of it like airport security working in two stages. A basic packet filter checks boarding passes at the gate, allowing safe ports like port 443 for H T T P S while blocking unused ports such as port 22. Deeper inside, a Web Application Firewall inspects the luggage itself, scanning H T T P payloads to catch cross-site scripting, S Q L injection, and bot floods. Closing unused ports keeps your attack surface small.
m5-management-privacy: Keeping user accounts safe takes both strong engineering and sharp habits. Never store plain passwords in browser localStorage, where any script on the page could read them. Real servers protect passwords using slow, salted hashes like bcrypt or Argon2 alongside Multi-Factor Authentication. For everyday browsing, watch out for phishing sites that imitate real brands on look-alike domains. Before entering any password or O T P, pause and verify the exact root domain and H T T P S padlock, and always respect user privacy rules.
m5-copyright: Just because an image, article, or piece of code is visible on a public website does not mean it is free to reuse. Everything published online is protected by copyright by default unless an explicit license says otherwise. Creative Commons licenses make sharing clear: C C Zero waives rights completely, while C C B Y lets you reuse work freely as long as you credit the creator. In software, M I T and Apache licenses allow reuse with notices, while G P L requires derivatives to stay open source. Always write your own code and credit your sources.
